title: TB9-15701
frame:
Forum: Refugee Appeal Division (appeal tribunal).
Parties: the appellant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review (from the opening paragraphs): The Refugee Appeal Division ("RAD") upholds the determination of the Refugee Protection Division ("RPD") that the Appellant is neither a Convention refugee nor a person in need of protection.
How the layers nest here: The RAD member is the author (layer 1). The appellant and the Minister make submissions to the RAD (layer 2). The RPD decision under appeal is layer 3, and what the claimant or the Minister said to the RPD, as reported, is layer 4.

paragraphs.text: These are my reasons for dismissing the appeal of XXXX XXXX XXXX ("the Appellant"). The Refugee Appeal Division ("RAD") upholds the determination of the Refugee Protection Division ("RPD") that the Appellant is neither a Convention refugee nor a person in need of protection.

The Appellant, a citizen of Nigeria, claims a fear of persecution based on her sexual orientation. In her Basis of Claim ("BOC") narrative, she alleged that her marriage ended after her husband discovered her relationship with another woman in 2012, and that in 2017, he threatened to report her to the police if she did not end her relationship with her then girlfriend. At the hearing, she further alleged that her husband threatened to go the police if she did not pay him XXXX XXXX naira, and that, since coming to Canada, her husband's extended family has issued threats against her. The RPD determined the Appellant was not credible. The Appellant challenges this determination on appeal.

Generally, I must review a decision of the RPD on a standard of correctness.1 The exception to this rule is where the RPD enjoys a meaningful advantage in assessing the credibility of oral testimony, which may attract deference in particular cases.2 In this case, however, the RPD had no advantage. I have therefore considered whether its decision was correct.

The Appellant seeks to admit the following new evidence on appeal: * Letter from XXXX XXXX XXXX ("XXXX"), XXXX XXXX XXXX, XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX, 26 June 2019 * Letter from XXXX, XXXX XXXX, XXXX XXXX XXXX, 27 June 2019 * Photos of the Appellant at XXXX choir and Pride, Undated * Affidavit of the Appellant, 12 July 2019

In assessing whether to admit new evidence, I must consider the statutory requirements of IRPA s. 110(4), i.e. whether the evidence arose after the rejection of the claim, or was not reasonably available, or could not reasonably have been expected in the circumstances to have been presented at the time of the rejection. I am also mindful of the Raza factors, which the Federal Court of Appeal confirmed in Singh are relevant to the assessment of new evidence before the RAD;3 namely, whether the evidence is new, credible, and relevant.

In this case, the Appellant has presented letters which post-date the RPD decision of 5 June 2019; however, they are not "new" in the sense that they simply reiterate evidence of the Appellant's participation in the XXXX XXXX XXXX since 2018, which was already before the RPD. The first letter, by XXXX XXXX XXXX, XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX, indicates that XXXX no longer issues supporting letters for refugee claims and confirms the Appellant's attendance at XXXX since July 2018.4 An attendance sheet showing attendance between July 2018 and February 2019 was in evidence before the RPD.5 This evidence is therefore not new; it was also open to the Appellant to provide evidence of her ongoing attendance before the RPD issued its decision on 5 June 2019.

Similarly, the letter of XXXX XXXX, XXXX XXXX XXXX, simply indicates that the Appellant has been involved with the XXXX choir since the fall of 2018.6 The Appellant testified to her involvement in the XXXX choir before the RPD.7 There also appear to have been photos of the Appellant at the XXXX choir in evidence before the RPD.8 There is no reason why she could not have provided a letter indicating her involvement in the XXXX choir before the RPD issued its decision. For these reasons, the letters are rejected.

The photos of the Appellant at the XXXX choir and Pride are undated; however, I acknowledge the Appellant's statement that the photos of Pride are from 2019 and so presumably post-date the RPD's decision of 5 June 2019. Given that the Pride photos depict the Appellant's involvement in LGBTQ events in Canada, they are broadly relevant to the appeal. For these reasons, they are accepted into evidence. Because the XXXX choir photos are undated, and it is not clear why the Appellant could not have provided these into evidence before the RPD, they are rejected. As noted above, it appears there were photos of the Appellant at choir before the RPD in any event.
Finally, the Appellant's affidavit simply takes issue with the RPD's findings; it is argument and not evidence and therefore is not admitted into evidence on appeal.

The Appellant has requested an oral hearing. The RAD can only hold a hearing if there is new evidence that raises a serious issue with respect to the Appellants' credibility, which is central to the decision in the claim, and, if accepted, would justify accepting or rejecting the claim.9 In this case, I do not find the photos of the Appellant at Pride 2019 events raise any serious questions of credibility determinative of the appeal. For this reason, there is no need to hold an oral hearing.

The determinative issue on appeal remains credibility. For the following reasons, I agree with the RPD that the Appellant has not met her burden to establish her claim. Evolving evidence of threats, decision to leave and reavailment undermine credibility

The Appellant provided evolving evidence on the threats from her husband in Nigeria. In her narrative, she indicated that he began threatening her "sometime in 2016" that if she did not end her relationship with her then girlfriend, he would go the police.10 In testimony, she indicated that he began threatening her in late 2016 or early 2017, and that he initially threatened to go to the police if she did not end her relationship, but then demanded she pay him XXXX XXXX naira or he would go to the police.11

As the RPD noted, the Appellant travelled to the United States and returned to Nigeria after her husband began threatening her.12 The Appellant explained at the hearing that she did not take her husband's threats seriously at that time and did not think of claiming protection in the US. According to her testimony, she did not decide to leave Nigeria permanently until she returned from her second trip to the US13 (which was in XXXX 2017),14 at which point she began take her husband's threats seriously. She testified that what changed for her was that her husband was demanding XXXX XXXX naira, which she did not have.15 However, this is inconsistent with her narrative, which says she was scared when her husband threatened to go to the police and which does not mention his demand for XXXX XXXX naira.16

The Appellant further contradicted herself when she testified that "the heat was not on" at the time she applied for a Canadian visa,17 which was in April 2018,18 because her husband had not yet demanded the XXXX XXXX naira,19 and that her intention when she applied was to simply attend the XXXX conference as indicated in her application.20 As the RPD pointed out, this is inconsistent with her narrative, in which she stated that when she heard about the XXXX conference she "prayed that [she would] be granted the visa, because [she had] heard on the news how Canada welcomes people whom their life is at risk" [sic].21 It is also inconsistent with her prior testimony that she decided to leave Nigeria permanently when she got back from the US the second time because her husband was demanding XXXX XXXX naira.22

The Appellant's submission that the RPD ignored her explanation that she did not take her husband's threats seriously when she was in the US is not persuasive; the panel considered the explanation but ultimately did not accept it. In light of the above, I find the Appellant's evolving evidence of the nature of the threats and when she began to take them seriously undermines her credibility, as does her reavailment to Nigeria after her husband began threatening her. Inconsistent testimony, lack of corroborative evidence about relationship with XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX

I am not persuaded by the Appellant's submission that the RPD erred when it found her testimony that her relationship with XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX "lasted more than 10 years" to be inconsistent with its actual length of 21 years. The Appellant argues on appeal that the panel failed to consider her testimony that the relationship was "off and on" during the 21-year timeframe; however, this was not the Appellant's evidence.

In her narrative, she indicated that after her marriage, she "lived happily because my girlfriend [XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX] is always at my home, helping me out wherever & whenever, most especially whenever I gave birth. She was the best friend of mine that was known by all, even, after I got married, we still remain friends."23 At the hearing, she testified that the relationship started "around '91" and "lasted, as long as I can remember, till 2012."24 When the panel asked if she maintained a "lover relationship" with XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX until 2012, the Appellant responded in the affirmative; while acknowledging it was not the same as when they were in school, she indicated they remained lovers and were romantic when the opportunity arose.25 With respect, the "on/off" nature of the relationship appears to be a post-rejection spin on the Appellant's evidence which is not borne out by the record.

Contrary to the Appellant's submission, the RPD did not err in requiring corroborative evidence of her 21-year relationship with XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX While the jurisprudence and SOGIE Guideline26 are clear that the Board cannot draw negative inferences solely on a claimant's failure to provide corroborating evidence, where there are valid reasons to doubt a claimant's credibility, the Board "may validly consider the failure to provide such documentation in making its credibility determination if it does not accept the claimant's explanation for that failure."27 In this case, there were valid reasons to doubt the Appellant's credibility.

At the hearing, the Appellant provided various explanations as to why she could not produce any corroborating evidence of her relationship with XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX, including that she no longer had the phone she used to exchange text messages, she was not an email person, she had not thought to keep any gifts or photos, the relationship did not end well, she had moved from the home she had been living in during their relationship, and that XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX was now married to a pastor and she did not want to approach her for evidence.28 The Appellant argues that the RPD ignored her explanations and imposed a Western standard by assuming she would actually use an email associated with her business registration.

While the lack of electronic communication and her desire not to interfere in XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX's marriage are reasonable enough on their own, I agree with the RPD that the complete lack of evidence of their decades-long relationship from the time they were in school together is not. To this end, I note that the Appellant submitted extensive records dating from the early 1990s into evidence, including school registration and admission documents dating from 1991;29 numerous receipts and certificates from her school dating between 1991 and 1993;30 photos of her wedding and family events, including photos dating from 1993, 1996, and 1997;31 and receipts for her store rent between 2005 and 2010.32 If XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX was as involved in her life as alleged in the narrative, including as her maid of honour at the wedding,33 it is reasonable to expect some surviving evidence of their decades-long relationship to have been presented. I agree with the RPD that given the Appellant's inconsistent testimony and lack of corroborating evidence, her relationship with XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX has not been established on a balance of probabilities.

Contrary to the Appellant's submission, this is not evidence of the panel seeking to reject the claim at all costs. Rather, given the significant credibility concerns identified with the Appellant's allegations, corroborative evidence would have helped to rehabilitate the claim. As the Court has held, "it is trite law that the applicant bears the onus of establishing the elements of [her] claim for protection."34 While a claimant need not demonstrate a prior relationship to establish a SOGIE claim, in this case, the Appellant's relationship with XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX is central to her allegations. It was her husband's discovery of this relationship which, she alleges, caused her marriage to break down and which eventually led to her husband's threats against her. The Appellant's failure to establish her relationship with XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX therefore calls into question her entire narrative. Failure to establish marriage breakdown

There is further reason to question whether the Appellant has actually separated from her husband. As the RPD pointed out, the Appellant provided inconsistent evidence about her living arrangements. In response to the panel's questioning, the Appellant indicated she had been at her current address since 2015 and had lived alone for about a year and a half.35 When asked to explain what her situation was for the other year and half, given she left Nigeria in 2018, she clarified her evidence to say she was living alone but her children were sometimes staying with her on weekends.36

The RPD drew a negative inference from this, noting that the Schedule A form listed the Appellant at this address for three years and it was reasonable to expect her to provide consistent testimony on how long she lived alone. The panel further noted that the Appellant listed her husband and children at this address in her visitor visa application, which she completed herself.37 It did not accept the Appellant's explanation that she did not know where her husband and children were living, so she listed them at her address as she did not want anyone at the XXXX club to know she was separated. The panel noted that while a desire for privacy is not unreasonable on its own, this explanation was not sufficient in light of the other credibility concerns identified in her claim.

The Appellant argues that the panel misconstrued her evidence on this issue, because she stated at the hearing that she lived alone for a year and a half and then her children were living with her on weekends for a year and a half. However, I agree with the RPD that the explanation is not sufficient to overcome the other credibility issues with respect to the Appellant's living situation. I further note that the Appellant's evidence is inconsistent with her son's email, which states that his father did not permit the children to spend the night at their mother's,38 and that the Appellant continued to use her previous address (where she listed herself as living from 2008 to 2015 on her Schedule A) in her driver's licence which was issued in June 2016;39 a 2018 tax receipt also places her at the previous address,40 as does a 2018 bank statement.41 While the Appellant filed a name change affidavit which stated she was returning to her maiden name,42 she continued to use her married name in the driver's licence which was issued in 2016.43 The name change affidavit also pre-dates her alleged date of separation, as it was commissioned in 2011. While not determinative, these further issues support the RPD's finding that the Appellant was not credible with respect to her living arrangements and the state of her relationship with her husband.

For all of these reasons, I find that the Appellant has failed to establish that her marriage broke down and she is separated from her husband, on a balance of probabilities. Other supporting documents insufficient to establish allegations

In light of the significant credibility concerns identified above, I agree with the RPD that the remaining supporting evidence is insufficient to establish the Appellant's allegations, on a balance of probabilities. This includes the emails and letter from her son and daughter;44 WhatsApp messages containing threats from her husband;45 and photos of the Appellant and another woman,46 whom she alleges was her girlfriend at the time her husband began threatening her.

The photos of the Appellant with another woman are not, on their own, sufficient to establish her sexual orientation. As the RPD noted, the name of the sender in the email from the Appellant's son does not match her son's name. The son's emails and daughter's email and letter are not accompanied by identity documents;47 the daughter's typed letter is neither signed nor dated. The source of the WhatsApp messages submitted into evidence before the RPD is not verifiable, as the panel noted. These issues limit the reliability of this evidence. Additionally, the WhatsApp message purporting to be from the Appellant's husband is not consistent with her allegations; it says that the Appellant left the home,48 whereas the Appellant's narrative indicates that it was her husband who left.49 Given these issues, I give the evidence from the Appellant's family little weight and do not find it sufficient to overcome the credibility issues in this claim. Sur place claim not made out

I acknowledge the Appellant's involvement in the XXXX XXXX XXXX as well as her attendance at Pride 2019.50 Given the significant credibility concerns outlined above, however, I do not find evidence of the Appellant's self-identification with the LGBTQ community in Canada sufficient to establish her sexual orientation, on a balance of probabilites.

I have also considered whether the Appellant would be perceived as bisexual upon return to Nigeria, regardless of her actual sexual orientation, and whether this would pose a risk upon return. However, given that she has failed to establish her allegations about what happened in Nigeria, I do not accept that her husband's family or the police are interested in her, on a balance of probabilities. Nor has any evidence been presented to suggest that the Appellant's involvement at XXXX or Pride events has come to the attention of the authorities in Nigeria.

For the reasons set out above, I dismiss the appeal and confirm the decision of the RPD that the Appellant is neither a Convention refugee nor a person in need of protection.
